lessons.objectiveEnglish: Ask a server or hotel host the basic questions you need at breakfast.
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Ask a server or hotel host the basic questions you need at breakfast, such as what something costs, where the restroom is, and what a dish is called.
lessons.focusEnglish: Question words (qu'est-ce que, qui, où, quand, combien, comment, pourquoi, quel or lequel) and est-ce que, which turns a statement into a question without changing the word order.
lessons.focusFrench: Mots interrogatifs : qu'est-ce que, qui, où, quand, combien, comment, pourquoi, quel / lequel ; est-ce que pour transformer une phrase en question.

words.noteEnglish: Quoi alone is short and informal. In a full question, use Qu'est-ce que... ? as in Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez ?
Qui is the same for one person or several. Qui nous sert ? means Who is serving us?
Où has an accent grave and means where.
Quand means when. Quand est-ce que... ? is also common in full questions.
Combien means how much or how many. Combien coûte... ? asks about a price.
Comment means how. Comment s'appelle... ? asks what something is called.
Pourquoi means why. Parce que means because, and it is two words.
Quel goes before a noun and agrees with it: quel café, quelle tasse. Lequel stands alone when you choose from options. Lequel changes form: laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles.
Inclus means included. If you are not sure, ask: Le petit-déjeuner est-il inclus ?
Viennoiserie is a broad French term for pastries such as croissants; local names vary.
Vous is the polite form with staff. Me means to me, and recommandez means you recommend.
Les toilettes is the usual café word for restroom. Sont is plural because toilettes is plural.
Coûter means to cost. Combien coûte... ? is the usual way to ask a price.
S'appeler means to be called. Cette agrees with the feminine noun viennoiserie.

words.fr: Quel est le café de la maison ?
words.noteEnglish: La maison means the house, so café de la maison is the house coffee. Quel is used before est.
Nous means us. Servir means to serve.

lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Ask a hotel host what breakfast costs, where the restroom is, and what this bread is called.
lessons.speakingFrench: Combien coûte le petit-déjeuner ? Où sont les toilettes ? Comment s'appelle ce pain ?

english: At the hotel, Emma and Tom ask: Who is serving us?
Rosa: I am serving you, what coffee do you want?
Tom: Which is the house coffee?
Rosa: It is the café de olla, why don't you try it?
Emma: How much is the breakfast and when does it end?
Rosa: It is the included breakfast and it ends at 11.
Tom points at the sweet bread: What is this bread called?
Emma: Where is the restroom?
Rosa: It is called a concha, and the restroom is on the right.
french: À l'hôtel, Emma et Tom demandent : Qui nous sert ?
Rosa : Je vous sers. Quel café voulez-vous ?
Tom : Quel est le café de la maison ?
Rosa : C'est notre café filtre maison, pourquoi ne pas le goûter ?
Emma : Combien coûte le petit-déjeuner, et quand se termine-t-il ?
Rosa : Le petit-déjeuner est inclus, et il se termine à 11 heures.
Tom montre une viennoiserie : Comment s'appelle cette viennoiserie ?
Emma : Où sont les toilettes ?
Rosa : C'est un pain au chocolat, et les toilettes sont à droite.
englishFrenchCourse: At the hotel, Emma and Tom ask: Who is serving us?
Rosa: I am serving you, what coffee do you want?
Tom: Which is the house coffee?
Rosa: It is our house filter coffee; why not try it?
Emma: How much is the breakfast and when does it end?
Rosa: It is the included breakfast and it ends at 11.
Tom points at a pastry: What is this pastry called?
Emma: Where is the restroom?
Rosa: It is a pain au chocolat, and the restroom is on the right.

teachingNotesEnglish: Question words: qui (who), où (where), quand (when), combien (how much), comment (how), pourquoi (why), quel / lequel (which). Qu'est-ce que... ? is the usual way to ask what.
Est-ce que can go in front of any statement to make it a question: Est-ce que le petit-déjeuner est inclus ? The statement word order stays the same.
Pourquoi (why) is one word. Parce que (because) is two words.
Quel agrees with the noun: quel café, quelle tasse, quels fruits. Lequel stands alone: Lequel voulez-vous ?
Use vous with hotel staff and with anyone you have just met.
authoringNotesEnglish: Title, objective, word en values and kinds, and English passage lines are preserved exactly from the source. The French-course title and objective are new English display text.

The hotel breakfast includes café de olla and concha, implying a Mexican setting. These names remain source-anchored loan terms. A future Francophone variant needs its own breakfast and currency details.
The sweet bread is rendered as pain sucré, a plain description. Native review should decide whether a French term is better for a café menu.
Source Spanish question words are replaced with French question words, and no Spanish grammar is carried over.
Native French review is open. reviewed:false.

lessons.objectiveEnglish: Say what you don't eat, say you are not ready yet, and ask for more, less or another.
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Say what you do not eat, say you are not ready yet, and ask for more, less or another at a café.
lessons.focusEnglish: Negation with ne ... pas, ne ... jamais, ne ... personne, ne ... rien and pas encore; amounts with plus de, moins de and un autre / une autre.
lessons.focusFrench: Négations : ne ... pas, ne ... jamais, ne ... personne, ne ... rien, pas encore ; plus de, moins de, un autre / une autre ; de après une négation.

words.noteEnglish: La viande is meat in general. Use le poulet for chicken or le bœuf for beef.
Les noix can mean walnuts or nuts in casual speech. For an allergy, ask about les fruits à coque (tree nuts) and les cacahuètes (peanuts) separately.
Cacahuète is the everyday French word for peanut. Arachide is also used, especially for the plant.
Laitier means dairy. Lait means milk.
Le gluten is the same word in French. Do not assume a dish is gluten-free; ask the kitchen.
Sans lactose means without lactose. Lait délactosé is also used on labels.
Ne ... personne means nobody. Ne goes before the verb and personne goes after it: Je ne vois personne.
Pas encore means not yet. Pas encore prêt means not ready yet.
Un autre is masculine and une autre is feminine: un autre café, une autre tasse.
Plus de + noun means more: plus de lait.
Moins de + noun means less: moins de sucre.

words.fr: Je ne mange pas de viande.
words.noteEnglish: Ne ... pas wraps the verb. After a negative verb, du, de la and des become de.

words.en: I never eat peanuts, I'm allergic.
words.fr: Je ne mange jamais de cacahuètes, je suis allergique.
words.noteEnglish: Ne ... jamais means never. Allergique has one form for everyone, so it does not change.

words.fr: Nous ne sommes pas encore prêts.
words.noteEnglish: Pas encore goes after the verb. Prêts becomes prêtes if everyone in the group is a woman.

words.fr: Un autre café, s'il vous plaît.
words.noteEnglish: Un autre is used before a masculine noun. S'il vous plaît is the polite closing.

words.en: More milk and less sugar, please.
words.fr: Plus de lait et moins de sucre, s'il vous plaît.
words.noteEnglish: Plus de and moins de are followed by a noun without an article.

words.en: I don't want anything else, thanks.
words.fr: Je ne veux rien d'autre, merci.
words.noteEnglish: French also uses a second negative word with ne: ne ... rien means nothing. Rien d'autre means nothing else.

lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Tell a server you are not ready yet, then say you don't eat meat and ask for another coffee with less sugar.
lessons.speakingFrench: Nous ne sommes pas encore prêts. Je ne mange pas de viande. Un autre café avec moins de sucre, s'il vous plaît.

passage.titleFrench: Un petit-déjeuner à Lyon avec des restrictions alimentaires
english: Emma and Tom are having breakfast at a café in Oaxaca.
The server Luis asks: Are you ready?
Emma: We're not ready yet.
Emma: I don't eat meat and Tom doesn't eat dairy products.
Tom: I never eat peanuts, I'm allergic.
Luis: I'm going to ask the kitchen if they use nuts or peanuts.
Luis: The green chilaquiles without cream or cheese have no meat or dairy.
Luis: The corn tortillas don't have gluten.
Emma: Another coffee with more lactose-free milk and less sugar, please.
french: Emma et Tom prennent le petit-déjeuner dans un café à Lyon.
Le serveur Luis demande : Vous êtes prêts ?
Emma : Nous ne sommes pas encore prêts.
Emma : Je ne mange pas de viande, et Tom ne mange pas de produits laitiers.
Tom : Je ne mange jamais de cacahuètes, je suis allergique.
Luis : Je vais demander à la cuisine quels ingrédients et ustensiles sont utilisés.
Luis : Je ne peux pas confirmer la préparation de ce plat.
Tom : Alors, je ne mange rien ici.
Emma : Un autre café avec moins de sucre, s'il vous plaît.
englishFrenchCourse: Emma and Tom are having breakfast at a café in Lyon.
The server Luis asks: Are you ready?
Emma: We're not ready yet.
Emma: I don't eat meat and Tom doesn't eat dairy products.
Tom: I never eat peanuts, I'm allergic.
Luis: I will ask the kitchen which ingredients and utensils are used.
Luis: I cannot confirm how this dish is prepared.
Tom: Then I won't eat anything here.
Emma: Another coffee with less sugar, please.

teachingNotesEnglish: Ne ... pas wraps the verb: je ne mange pas. Before a vowel, ne becomes n': je n'aime pas.
After a negative verb, du, de la, des and un / une become de: je ne mange pas de viande.
Ne ... jamais means never. Ne ... personne means nobody. Ne ... rien means nothing. Ne goes before the verb and the second word goes after it.
Pas encore means not yet: Nous ne sommes pas encore prêts.
Plus de and moins de + noun mean more and less: plus de lait, moins de sucre.
Prêts agrees with the group: prêts for a group of men or mixed people, prêtes for a group of women.

Allergy language practice: a menu, label or ingredient answer alone does not establish suitability. Tom declines food because staff cannot confirm preparation or cross-contact. Qualified allergy review remains required.
For a peanut allergy, say Je suis allergique aux cacahuètes. Aux is the contraction of à + les. Ask staff about ingredients and cross-contact; do not assume an item is safe.
authoringNotesEnglish: Title, objective, word en values and kinds, and English passage lines are preserved exactly from the source.

The source English passage contains unverified allergen claims. English anchors remain unchanged as provenance. French dialogue has the server say he will check with the kitchen; no safety claim should be treated as a guarantee.
This lesson must not be used as allergy information for learners. The gluten and dairy claims need verification by the restaurant before any real-world reliance.
Setting: Oaxaca, Mexico, is kept because the source reading names it. Peanuts are cacahuètes in French. A future France, Québec or Belgium variant needs local café details.
Native French review is open. reviewed:false.

lessons.objectiveEnglish: Ask a server politely for the bill, water or the check, and give simple usted commands.
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Ask a server politely for the bill, water or cream, and say you will pay and keep the change.
lessons.focusEnglish: Polite requests with Pourriez-vous ... ? and Pouvez-vous ... ?, plus je vous laisse for leaving a tip. Use vous with staff and do not use bare command forms.
lessons.focusFrench: Demandes polies avec pourriez-vous ... ? et pouvez-vous ... ? ; je vous laisse la monnaie ; vocabulaire de l'addition, du paiement et du pourboire.

words.noteEnglish: L'addition is the bill in a café or restaurant. Say l'addition, s'il vous plaît.
Le pourboire is a tip. Check whether service is included and local practice; no tip is assumed or required by this fictional scene.
La carte alone can also mean the menu. For a bank card, say la carte bancaire.
Les espèces is the everyday word for cash. En espèces means paid in cash.
La monnaie means coins or change. Le change means currency exchange, so it is a different word.
Des glaçons are ice cubes. La glace means ice in general and also ice cream.
Le sel is salt. Le poivre is pepper.
La paille is the common French word for a drinking straw.
La crème is cream. Crème fraîche is thicker and tangier.

words.en: Could you bring me the bill, please?
words.fr: Pourriez-vous m'apporter l'addition, s'il vous plaît ?
words.noteEnglish: Pourriez-vous is a polite request with vous, softer than a command. M' is me before a vowel.

words.en: Can you give me a glass of water?
words.fr: Pouvez-vous me donner un verre d'eau ?
words.noteEnglish: Donner means to give. Un verre d'eau means a glass of water.

words.fr: Pourriez-vous m'apporter un peu plus de crème, s'il vous plaît ?
words.noteEnglish: Un peu plus de + noun means a little more. The polite question replaces a bare command.

words.fr: Pourriez-vous patienter un instant, s'il vous plaît ?
words.noteEnglish: Patienter means to wait. Un instant means a moment.
Laisser means to leave or keep something. Je vous laisse la monnaie is a common way to leave the change as a tip.

lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Ask a server for a glass of water and the bill, pay in cash, and tell them to keep the change.
lessons.speakingFrench: Pourriez-vous me donner un verre d'eau ? Pourriez-vous m'apporter l'addition, s'il vous plaît ? Je paie en espèces. Je vous laisse la monnaie.

english: Anna eats eggs and coffee for breakfast at a café in Oaxaca.
Anna: Can you give me a glass of water?
Luis, the server, brings water with ice and a straw.
Anna: Can you bring me the salt, please?
Anna: Please bring me more cream.
Anna: Could you bring me the bill, please?
Luis: Are you going to pay by card or in cash?
Anna: In cash, here are 200 pesos.
Anna: Keep the change as a tip.
french: Anna prend des œufs et un café pour le petit-déjeuner dans un café à Lyon.
Anna : Pourriez-vous me donner un verre d'eau ?
Luis, le serveur, apporte de l'eau avec des glaçons et une paille.
Anna : Pourriez-vous m'apporter le sel, s'il vous plaît ?
Anna : Pourriez-vous m'apporter un peu plus de crème, s'il vous plaît ?
Anna : Pourriez-vous m'apporter l'addition, s'il vous plaît ?
Luis : Vous allez payer par carte ou en espèces ?
Anna : En espèces, voici vingt euros pour une addition de dix-huit euros.
Anna : Je vous laisse les deux euros de monnaie comme pourboire.
englishFrenchCourse: Anna has eggs and coffee for breakfast at a café in Lyon.
Anna: Can you give me a glass of water?
Luis, the server, brings water with ice and a straw.
Anna: Can you bring me the salt, please?
Anna: Please bring me more cream.
Anna: Could you bring me the bill, please?
Luis: Are you going to pay by card or in cash?
Anna: In cash, here are twenty euros for an eighteen-euro bill.
Anna: I will leave the two euros in change as a tip.

teachingNotesEnglish: Pourriez-vous + infinitive is a polite request: Pourriez-vous m'apporter l'addition ? (Could you bring me the bill?)
Pourriez-vous is the conditional of pouvoir with vous. Pouvez-vous is the present-tense version, a little more direct but still polite.
Me or m' comes before the verb: me donner, m'apporter.
Tipping customs differ by place. Ask whether service is included and check local practice before leaving a tip.
Je vous laisse la monnaie is a natural way to leave the change as a tip.
This lesson prefers polite question forms. Gardez la monnaie is also a natural vous imperative for 'keep the change'; an imperative with vous is not automatically rude.
authoringNotesEnglish: The source usted commands are adapted into polite vous requests and a natural change/tip phrase. The English anchors remain exact provenance.
The English anchors are preserved exactly, including the English command wording such as Please bring me and Keep the change.
The 200 pesos figure and Oaxaca setting are source-anchored. No conversion is applied. A France or Québec variant would need euros or Canadian dollars.
Native French review is open for Je vous laisse la monnaie as a tipping phrase. reviewed:false.

lessons.titleEnglish: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objectiveEnglish: Spot Spanish words you already know and use survival phrases when you don't understand.
lessons.titleFrenchCourseEnglish: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Spot French words that look like English and use survival phrases when you don't understand.
lessons.focusEnglish: Cognates ending in -tion, -té and -ent, plus survival phrases for getting help: I don't understand, speak more slowly, what are the ingredients, and emergency.
lessons.focusFrench: Mots apparentés en -tion, -té et -ent ; phrases de survie : je ne comprends pas, parler plus lentement, quels sont les ingrédients, Au secours.

words.noteEnglish: Réservation is close to English reservation. The verb is réserver: J'ai réservé.
Option is close to English. Végétarien agrees with the noun: végétarienne for feminine words.
Information is feminine. Des informations is also common for several pieces of information.
Spécialité is a close cognate. La spécialité du jour means today's specialty.
Variété is close to English variety. Une variété de means a variety of.
Ingrédient is a close cognate, and the word is plural in both languages.
Différent agrees with the noun: différent for masculine, différente for feminine.
Excellent has the same spelling. For feminine nouns, use excellente.
Une urgence means an emergency. Learn and verify the local emergency number before travel.
Excusez-moi is the polite form with staff. Comprendre means to understand.

words.en: Can you speak more slowly, please?
words.fr: Pourriez-vous parler plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ?
words.noteEnglish: Plus lentement means more slowly. Parler means to speak.

words.en: How do you say this in Spanish?
words.fr: Comment est-ce qu'on dit ça en français ?
words.noteEnglish: The source English anchor refers to Spanish; the learner-facing French-course question is 'How do you say this in French?' On dit means one says.
words.enFrenchCourse: How do you say this in French?

words.noteEnglish: Quels is the plural of quel. Sont is the plural of être (to be).

words.fr: Est-ce qu'il y a une option végétarienne ?
words.noteEnglish: Il y a means there is or there are. Est-ce que puts it in question form.
Au secours means help! Use it in a real emergency and call the local emergency number.

lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Tell a server you don't understand, ask them to speak more slowly, and ask what the ingredients of the specialty are.
lessons.speakingFrench: Excusez-moi, je ne comprends pas. Pourriez-vous parler plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ? Quels sont les ingrédients de la spécialité ?

english: Emma has a reservation at 9 at Café Luna.
On the wall there is emergency information in English and Spanish.
Rosa: Today's specialty is different: chilaquiles with chicken.
Emma: Excuse me, I don't understand.
Emma: Can you speak more slowly, please?
Emma: What are the ingredients?
Rosa: The ingredients are tortillas, green salsa, chicken and cheese.
Emma: Is there a vegetarian option?
Rosa: Yes, the vegetarian option is excellent and has a variety of vegetables.
french: Emma a une réservation à 9 heures au Café Luna.
Sur le mur, il y a des informations d'urgence en anglais et en espagnol.
Rosa : La spécialité du jour est différente : chilaquiles au poulet.
Emma : Excusez-moi, je ne comprends pas.
Emma : Pourriez-vous parler plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ?
Emma : Quels sont les ingrédients ?
Rosa : Les ingrédients sont des tortillas, de la salsa verde, du poulet et du fromage.
Emma : Est-ce qu'il y a une option végétarienne ?
Rosa : Oui, l'option végétarienne est excellente et il y a une variété de légumes.

teachingNotesEnglish: Many French words look like English: -tion (information, réservation), -té (variété), -ent (différent, excellent). Check the gender before you use them.
Survival phrases: Excusez-moi, je ne comprends pas. Pourriez-vous parler plus lentement ? Comment est-ce qu'on dit ça en français ?
Each survival phrase uses vous with staff.
Au secours is for a real emergency. Learn the local emergency number before travel.
authoringNotesEnglish: The source focus cognate endings (-ción, -dad, -ente) are Spanish spelling patterns, so they are replaced with French patterns (-tion, -té, -ent). The source word list is preserved.
The English anchor How do you say this in Spanish? remains exact source provenance. Use enFrenchCourse as its learner-facing English display text; runtime wiring is still pending.
No emergency number is stated as fact. Verify local emergency contacts before any travel or safety guidance.

The source reading names Café Luna and says the wall has emergency information in English and Spanish. Its precise location is unspecified; the French passage preserves those facts. A Francophone variant needs different context.
Native French review is open. reviewed:false.
